# Sequence Quality Control Assessment with FastQC

date: Spe 22, 2025
author: Stefanie Moreno

## Objective:

The purpose of this project is to demonstrate a quality control assessment of WGS reads 
with FastQC, Trimmomatic, Samtools, BWA, . 

## Background:

After reads are sequenced by NGS technologies,the data is returned in a FastQ 
file, which contains both the sequences and the quality information. Similar to FASTA, the 
FASTQ file begins with a header line, but the FASTQ header is denoted by 
an @ symbol. For a single record (sequence read), there are four lines, each of which is 
described below:

Line	Description

1	Always begins with ‘@’, followed by information about the read

2	The actual DNA sequence

3	Always begins with a ‘+’, and sometimes the same info as in line 1

4	Has a string of characters representing the quality scores; must have the same number of 
    characters as line 2. Line 4 has characters encoding the quality of each nucleotide in the
    read.

The legend below provides the mapping of quality scores (Phred-33) to the quality encoding 
characters. Different quality encoding scales exist (differing by offset in the ASCII table), 
but note the most commonly used one is fastqsanger, which is the scale output by Illumina since 
mid-2011.

    Quality encoding:  !"#$%&'()*+,-./0123456789:;<=>?@ABCDEFGHI
                       |         |         |         |         |
        Quality score: 0........10........20........30........40           

Each quality score represents the probability that the corresponding nucleotide call is 
incorrect. This quality score is logarithmic-based and is calculated as:

    Q = -10 x log10(P), where P is the probability that a base call is erroneous

These probability values are the results from the base calling algorithm and dependent on how
much signal was captured for the base incorporation. The score values can be interpreted as 
follows:

    Phred Quality Score	| Probability of incorrect base call  |	 Base call accuracy

        10      	                1 in 10	                        90%

        20	                        1 in 100	                    99%

        30	                        1 in 1000	                    99.9%

        40	                        1 in 10,000	                    99.99%

FastQC provides a simple way to do some quality checks on raw sequence data coming from 
high-throughput sequencing pipelines. It provides a modular set of analyses, which can be
used to obtain an impression of whether the data has any problems that should be addressed
before moving on to the next analysis. 

FastQC:

* Accepts FASTQ files (or BAM files) as input.
* Generates summary graphs and tables to help assess your data.
* Generates an easy-to-view HTML-based report with the graphs and tables.

## Steps of the Project:

To begin, I set up and activated a new micromamba environment in my terminal called bioinfo. 
I then accessed and downloaded the pre-compiled, raw FASTQ files for the E. coli dataset 
SRR25083113 directly from the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA). All commands used in the 
terminal can be found in the project file "bash_commands.sh". After the downloads were
completed, I accessed the FastQC platform.

Prior to transferring to the FastQC platform, I navigated into my home folder and unzipped
the two FastQ files. I then transitioned to the FAstQC platform and opened the first file.
Because of the size of the files, it took some time to process. Upon completing, I saved
each report as an html file.

## FastQC Plot Interpretations:

Within the FastQC report, a summary of all of the modules is given on the left-hand side. Modules with a green check represent data of sufficient quality. Red or yellow are not necessarily bad, but rather, they indicate modules that should be checked.

The first module gives the basic statistics for the sample. Generally, it is a good idea to keep track of the total number of reads sequenced for each sample and to make sure the read length and %GC content are as expected.
